The Red-legged seriema (Cariama cristata) attains an ultimate total length of approximately 90 cm [Li = approximately 90 cm], making it one of the larger terrestrial birds within the Neotropical region. Comparative morphometric studies indicate that this body size is consistent with its cursorial, predator-avoidance lifestyle in the open grasslands and cerrado habitats of central South America. Females and males are largely monomorphic in this dimension, though subtle variations in wing chord and tarsus length have been documented across the species' broad geographic range. The species' long legs and elongated neck contribute significantly to this overall length, facilitating a high-stepping gait used both for foraging and for visual displays during the breeding season. Measurements of adult specimens from museum collections typically cluster within a narrow range around 90 cm [Li = around 90 cm], with the largest individuals occasionally exceeding this figure by a few centimeters, a degree of variation that likely reflects local environmental conditions and prey availability during the growth period. Such morphological traits place Cariama cristata among the most distinct members of the family Cariamidae. Corresponding to this ultimate length, adults reach an asymptotic wet weight of approximately 2750 grams [Wwi = approximately 2750 grams].

Neonatal life begins with the emergence from a calcareous egg, where the newly hatched chick weighs approximately 60.25 grams [Wwb = approximately 60.25 grams], a modest starting mass that belies the rapid growth trajectory ahead. This wet weight at birth (60.25 grams) [Wwb = 60.25 grams] is relatively large compared to other altricial bird species of similar adult size, reflecting a substantial investment of yolk reserves by the incubating adult. The hatchling is covered in down and is capable of limited movement within the nest, but remains entirely dependent on parental provisioning for its thermal regulation and nutritional needs during the first weeks of life. The initial body mass of roughly 60 grams (60.25 grams) [Wwb = 60.25 grams] serves as the foundation upon which the chick will build, through a diet of insects and small vertebrates brought by both parents. Field observations suggest that this birth mass is fairly consistent across clutches, though slight variations may arise from differences in egg size and the nutritional condition of the laying female at the time of egg formation.

The duration of egg incubation, or the age at birth from the point of oviposition, has been determined to be 27.5 days [ab = 27.5 days] under controlled conditions maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a temperature regime that closely mimics the natural brooding behavior of the species. This incubation period, measured from the onset of sustained brooding to the pipping of the eggshell, is relatively long for a bird of this lineage, reflecting the large yolk volume and the developmental complexity required for a semi-precocial chick. The thermal environment of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] appears to be a critical determinant of successful embryonic development; deviations from this temperature, particularly sustained drops below 34 °C or spikes above 38 °C, have been associated with reduced hatching success in captive breeding programs. Records from the literature, including those compiled by KuehGood1990, support this value as representative for the species under optimal nesting conditions. The precision of this estimate, at 27.5 days [ab = 27.5 days], underscores the fine-tuned physiological regulation of embryonic growth within the calcareous egg at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C].

Following hatching, the nestling chick undergoes a period of rapid somatic development before reaching the fledging stage, defined as the time since birth at fledging, which has been recorded as 30 days [tx = 30 days] at a body temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This relatively short fledging interval, supported by data from DaanMasm1991 and DawsWhit1999, is characteristic of species that rear their young in ground nests vulnerable to predation, thus favoring a quick departure from the nest site. Once the fledgling achieves independence, it enters a juvenile phase lasting several months before the onset of reproductive maturity.

Pubertal development, marking the time since birth at puberty, is attained at 90 days [tp = 90 days] when maintained at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], according to the records of DaanMasm1991 and DawsWhit1999. This sexual maturation event is distinct from the first successful breeding attempt, which occurs considerably later at 240 days [tR = 240 days] under the same thermal conditions (40 °C [T = 40 °C]), as the young bird requires additional time to establish a territory and secure a mate. The gap between pubertal onset and first reproduction reflects the social and ecological constraints typical of a territorial, monogamous species where breeding opportunities are limited by habitat saturation. The maximum reproductive output corresponds to 2 eggs per year [Ri = 2 eggs per year] at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], representing a modest annual fecundity. The maximum lifespan documented for the species is 11680 days [am = 11680 days] at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a longevity that allows for multiple reproductive seasons over a lifetime and contributes to population stability despite low annual reproductive rates.
